hints: Think about what you need to see lots of cells at once: do you want to zoom right in on one cell, or zoom out to get a wide view?
Remember how to find total magnification from the two lenses, and how total magnification relates to the size of the field of view.
walkthrough:
**Link cells seen to field of view**

To see the greatest number of cells, you need the widest field of view. Think zooming out, not zooming in.

A wider view shows more cells, but each cell looks smaller.

**Calculate total magnification**

Total magnification controls how zoomed in you are:
$$\text{total magnification} = \text{eyepiece magnification} \times \text{objective magnification}$$

Lower total magnification gives a wider field of view, so more cells fit in.

**Pick the lowest magnification**

A: $5 \times 10 = \times 50$
B: $5 \times 40 = \times 200$
C: $10 \times 10 = \times 100$
D: $10 \times 40 = \times 400$

Option A has the lowest total magnification at only $\times 50$, so it gives the largest field of view and shows the most cells.

options.A: Correct, $\times 50$ is the lowest total magnification, so it gives the widest field of view and fits in the greatest number of cells.
options.B: Gives $\times 200$, which is higher magnification and a smaller field of view than A, so fewer cells are seen.
options.C: Gives $\times 100$, which is double the magnification of A, so the field of view is smaller and shows fewer cells.
options.D: Gives $\times 400$, the highest magnification, so it shows the greatest detail but the smallest field of view and fewest cells.
